# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-3 (Extended v60)

## Setting and Time
- Multiple time periods: French Revolution era; Napoleonic coronation epoch; 1809 (Pope's arrest); 1811 (Bishop's synod); 1813 onward (Napoleon's decline); 1815 (Bishop's 75th birthday, early October—evening/night of Valjean's theft and flight; **Battle of Waterloo/Hougomont siege, June 17-18, 1815; June 18-19 evening/night post-battle looting and conditions**); 1817 (carrier sighting; young Parisians' Saint-Cloud excursion); 1818 spring (Montfermeil cook-shop, Thénardier family, Fantine's arrival); 1819-1821 (Madeleine's mayoral appointment and town transformation); **1823 January (Fantine's arrest and street incident; Javert's revelation; Valjean's acute crisis; TRIAL SEQUENCE: Journey to Arras through February, arriving evening near eight o'clock; TRIAL EVENING SESSION; witnesses testify; Valjean reveals himself; acquittal of Champmathieu; arrest order issued; RETURN TO M. SUR M. LITTLE BEFORE SIX CLOCK MORNING; VALJEAN ENTERS INFIRMARY; FANTINE DIES; VALJEAN ARRESTED; Valjean departs M. sur M. marching toward Paris carrying bundle, dressed in workman's blouse)**; **1815 June 18-19 (midnight onward: post-Waterloo looting; mysterious prowler in blouse on hollow road of Ohain; sutler's wagon hidden behind hovel at Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud road angle; woman seated in wagon among coffers and packages)**; **autumn of the first year / 1815 onward (trial aftermath reflected; current narrative time at Dunstead harbor town)**; 1823 October (ship Orion enters Toulon port after heavy weather, for repairs; employed later at Brest as school-ship, part of Mediterranean squadron); **1823 Spanish campaign (war of conquest, corruption alleged, Bourbons misinterpreted as success, led to 1830 revolution)**; 1827 February (M. de Villèle parliamentary remarks on tax collection); 1849 (chapel walls freshly whitewashed); 1861/1862 (narrative reflection, traveller departing from Nivelles toward La Hulpe)
- Primary locations: M. sur M.; Montfermeil; Arras; Nivelles; La Hulpe; Braine-l'Alleud; Lillois; Genappe; Hal; Tongres; **Hougomont (château, farm, chapel, well, orchard, garden, wood, northern and southern doors, paddock, spiral staircase, chapel with wooden crucifix and Saint Anne statue); Mont-Saint-Jean plateau; Belle-Alliance; Abbey of Villiers forest; Rossomme farm; village of Ohain; hollow road of Ohain (from Braine-l'Alleud); Chapelle-Saint-Lambert; Wavre; Dion-le-Mont; Plancenoit; forest of Paris; Papelotte; Frischemont; Boitsfort; Groenendael; Soignes forest; Waterloo battlefield; Dunstead (harbor town); Montfermeil forest; forge; clearings and thickets; Toulon port; Brest; Mediterranean; Trocadéro; Spain**; England (Hampstead, Hull, Liverpool, Dunstead/Kelford, Suffolk, London, Welbeck Street, Lowestoft, Torton, Kelmere, Dunby, Yarlby, Ostcombe, Ravenmere); Kelmere (river crossing); meadow near Genappe; willow at Wilwick; Vincennes; Schoenbrunn; Philippi; Longwood; Saint Helena; Vienna; Pas de Calais; Abbey of Saint-Georges de Bocherville (near Rouen); Rouen

## Waterloo Battle: Strategic Analysis, Conditions, Course, Outcome, and Philosophical Meaning
- **June 18-19 Evening/Night: Post-Battle Conditions and Looting**
  - English established bivouac beyond Rossomme (sign of victory)
  - Prussians pushed forward on retreating rout
  - Wellington drew up report at Waterloo village to Lord Bathurst
  - **Narrative irony**: Waterloo village took no part, lay half league from scene; Mont-Saint-Jean cannonaded, Hougomont burned, La Haie-Sainte taken, Papelotte burned, Plancenoit burned, La Belle-Alliance—these names hardly known; Waterloo bears all honor
  - Hougomont and La Haie-Sainte burning at night, two great flames joined by English bivouac fire cordon like necklace of rubies with carbuncles
  - **Sixty thousand men killed; quietly rotted in following days, shedding peace over world**
  - Prompt stripping of dead bodies; dawn following battle reveals naked corpses
  - **Philosophical debate**: Some philosophers affirm same men who make glory plunder fallen; hero of day is vampire of night; hand plucking laurels cannot purloin shoes from corpse
  - **Mysterious looting (midnight onward)**: Man prowling toward hollow road of Ohain, neither English/French/peasant/soldier—ghoul attracted by scent, clad in blouse, no sack but large pockets, scrutinized corpses, rose and fled; sliding motion resembled twilight larvae (Norman legends call them "Alleurs")
  - **Hidden sutler's wagon**: Small wagon with fluted wicker hood, hidden behind hovel at Mont-Saint-Jean to Braine-l'Alleud angle; woman seated on coffers/packages; **CLAIM**: connection between wagon and prowler
  - **Hollow road conditions (evening June 18)**: Edges encumbered with horses/riders, inextricably heaped; corpses levelled road with plain, reached brim like filled bushel; heap in upper part, river of blood in lower; blood ran to Nivelles highway, overflowed in large pool before abatis of trees (spot still pointed out)
  - **Destruction of cuirassiers (Genappe road direction)**: Thickness of body layer proportioned to hollow road depth; at level middle point where Delort's division passed, layer thinner
  - **Officer rescue from heap (shadows of hollow road)**: Mysterious figure bent, fumbled among heap, seized and freed hand/arm/head, pulled out lifeless or unconscious man—a cuirassier officer of considerable rank; large gold epaulette beneath cuirass; no helmet; furious sword-cut scarred face, blood obscured features

## Post-Waterloo and Restoration Era (1815-1823)
- **1815 as "lugubrious April"**: Ancient unhealthy realities masked with new appearances; lie wedded 1789; right divine masked under charter; fictions became constitutional; prejudices, superstitions, mental reservations varnished with liberalism
- **Napoleon's lingering influence**: Populace sought him; when told "Napoleon is dead," veteran cried "you don't know him"; imagination distrusted him even overthrown; depths of Europe full of darkness; something enormous remained empty through disappearance
- **New France**: Future bore Liberty's star; young generations turned glowing eyes toward it; paradox—people loved simultaneously future/Liberty and past/Napoleon; defeat rendered vanquished greater; Bonaparte fallen seemed loftier than Napoleon erect
- **Napoleon's captivity**: Guarded by Hudson Lowe at Saint Helena; watched by Montchenu; folded arms became uneasiness to thrones; Alexander called him "my sleeplessness"; terror from quantity of revolution contained in him; phantom made old world tremble; kings reigned ill at ease with rock of Saint Helena on horizon
- **Congress of Vienna and Restoration (1815)**: Treaties made; Europe called this the Restoration
- **Restoration masquerade**: Constitutional language masks ancien régime realities

## 1823 Spanish Campaign (War of Succession, Historical Corruption)
- **Ship Orion arrival (October 1823)**: Entered Toulon port after heavy weather, damaged, for repairs; employed later at Brest as school-ship, part of Mediterranean squadron; received regulation salute of eleven guns, returned shot for shot; total twenty-two guns
- **Critique of military ceremony**: Civilized world discharges approximately one hundred fifty thousand useless shots daily across earth through salves, royal/military politeness, courteous exchanges, signals of etiquette, formalities, sunrises/sunsets; at six francs per shot equals nine hundred thousand francs daily, three hundred millions annually, vanishing in smoke; **meanwhile poor died of hunger**
- **Spanish campaign military analysis**: Taking of Trocadéro was fine military action; trumpets gave cracked sound; whole effect suspicious; history approves France for difficulty accepting false triumph; certain Spanish officers charged with resistance yielded too easily; corruption connected with victory; generals/not battles won; conquering soldier returned humiliated; debasing war; Bank of France readable in flag folds
- **Democratic perspective**: War wounded military spirit of France, enraged democratic spirit; enterprise of enthralment; French soldier (son of democracy) conquered yoke for others—hideous contradiction; France made to arouse nations' souls, not stifle them; all European revolutions since 1792 are French Revolution; liberty darts rays from France—solar fact; Bonaparte said this
- **Outrage on Revolution**: War of 1823 was outrage on generous Spanish nation AND outrage on French Revolution; France committed monstrous violence; except wars of liberation, everything armies do is by foul means; "passive obedience" indicates this; army strange masterpiece where force results from enormous sum of impotence; war made by humanity against humanity, despite humanity

## Bourbons' Strategic Error and 1830 Consequence
- **Misinterpretation as success (1823)**: Bourbons took Spanish campaign for success; did not perceive danger in having idea slain to order; in innocence introduced immense enfeeblement of crime into establishment as element of strength; spirit of ambush entered their politics
- **1830 had germ in 1823**: Spanish campaign became argument for force/adventures by right Divine in Bourbon counsels; France having re-established "el rey netto" in Spain might re-establish absolute king at home; fell into alarming error of taking soldier obedience for nation consent; such confidence ruins thrones; not permitted to sleep in shadow of machineel tree nor in shadow of army

## Valjean Trial Aftermath and Flight (1823)
- **Newspaper account**: M. Madeleine (stranger in Pas de Calais) resuscitated ancient local jet/black glass trinket industry; made fortune; appointed mayor; discovered to be ex-convict Jean Valjean, condemned 1796 for theft, who broke ban
- **Money disposition**: Before arrest, Valjean withdrew over half million francs from M. Laffitte (legitimately acquired in business); concealment location unknown
- **Trial and sentencing**: Theft proved committed in complicity with others; Valjean member of robber band in south; pronounced guilty; condemned to death penalty; **refused appeal; king commuted to penal servitude for life; immediately taken to Toulon prison**
- **Economic consequences (1827)**: State perceived someone crushed; less than four years after Court of Assizes judgment, tax collection costs doubled in M. sur M. arrondissement; M. de Villèle noted fact in parliament February 1827

## Montfermeil/Dunstead Community: Boulatruelle's Forest Activity and Daily Life

**Boulatruelle's Mysterious Search (Late 1823 or ongoing)**:
- **Recent behavior**: Quit road-breaking/care tasks early; betook himself to forest with pickaxe; encountered toward evening in deserted clearings, wildest thickets; appeared searching for something, sometimes digging holes
- **Public perception**: Goodwives initially took him for Beelzebub; recognized him, not reassured; encounters caused Boulatruelle lively displeasure; sought to hide; mystery evident in actions
- **Speculation**: Some surmised no fabulous treasure of legends, but fine windfall more serious/palpable than devil's bank-bills; road-mender half discovered secret
- **Local investigation**: Schoolmaster and Thénardier (tavern proprietor, everybody's friend) became "puzzled," allied themselves with Boulatruelle; schoolmaster affirmed in former times law would have instituted inquiry, forced him to speak, tortured if necessary, water test applied; Thénardier: "Let us put him to the wine test"
- **Drinking interrogation**: Made effort to get Boulatruelle drinking; drank enormous amount, said very little; combined gormandizer's thirst with judge's discretion; by returning to charge, comparing/putting together obscure words, Thénardier and schoolmaster imagined they made out [CLAIM: content not fully revealed in text]
- **Background**: Former galley convict; peculiar ways in forest; subjected to police supervision; employed as road-mender at reduced rates on crossroad Gagny-Lagny; viewed with disfavor as too respectful/humble/cap-removing/trembling before gendarmes; suspected of lying in ambush at copse verges at nightfall; affiliated to robber bands (claim); drunkard

**Dunstead Community Daily Life (Autumn period, ongoing contemporary narrative)**:
- **Minor figures and scattered actions**:
  - **Nylia Corrford**: complained of aching back, as usual
  - **Marald Corrford**: asked "Will it rain, do you think?"; Kassa shrugged; later mended torn sleeve by window, said little
  - **Ulrald Corrford**: complained of aching back; **gave Lura Haskick solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Stenson family** (COMMITMENT); counted coins twice, came up penny short; later laughed at story nobody else found funny (name variation: Yedan Corrford laughed at same story)
  - **Yewyn Corrford**: appeared tired (Kassa noted this); bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; agreed with Kassa about salt price scandal
  - **Lura Haskick**: recipient of Ulrald's debt-payment promise; later mended torn sleeve by window, said little
  - **Pewyn Stenenridge**: laughed at story nobody else found funny; later talked of nothing much with Thizek—weather, harvest, lame horse
  - **Elra**: spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight; walked long way round to avoid muddy square
  - **Rozek Stenenridge**: burned letter after reading; later found work in Staveford, moved there, did not return to Dunstead; **CLAIM**: Luena followed him to Staveford within the month
  - **Yera Haskick**: revealed in letter (burned by Rozek) that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood
  - **Kassa Brackick**: told Yewyn "The price of salt is a scandal" (agreed)
  - **Peten**: asked "Will it rain, do you think?"; Yewyn only shrugged
  - **Stenson family**: owed debt by Ulrald

**Mundane Environmental Details**: Ruts and puddles after thaw; crooked sun chalked on forge wall; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long; frost silvered hedges overnight; bell for vespers rang thinly across roofs; children chased hoop down lane shrieking; cart loaded with turnips creaked past well

## Main Characters Status (January 1823 onward)

**Jean Valjean / M. Madeleine—IMPRISONED AT TOULON**
- Arrested M. sur M., returned to Toulon; whereabouts confined

**Fantine—DEAD, BURIED IN PAUPER'S GRAVE**
- Died in infirmary; received pauper's burial

**Cosette**—At Montfermeil with Thénardiers; awaiting rescue

**Napoleon Bonaparte—DEFEATED, IMPRISONED AT SAINT HELENA**
- Waterloo defeat June 18, 1815; guarded by Hudson Lowe; watched by Montchenu; symbol of revolution; terror to restored monarchies

## Metaphysical Reflection: Ship of the Line
- Ship of the line composed of heaviest/lightest matter; deals with three substance forms: solid, liquid, fluid; battles all three; eleven iron claws seize granite seabed; wings/antennae catch wind; breath through one hundred twenty cannons replies to thunder; ocean seeks to lead astray; vessel has soul/compass counseling it, showing north; lanterns supply stars in blackest nights; against wind: cordage/canvas; against water: wood; against rocks: iron/brass/lead; against shadows: light; against immensity: needle

## Themes
- Destiny and chance; divine intervention transcending human agency
- Waterloo as historical hinge: end of military monarchy, beginning of modern age
- War's moral paradox and waste: ceremony costs fortunes while poor starve; corruption endemic to military enterprise
- Restoration as masquerade and seeds of revolution: 1823 campaign produced 1830 consequence
- Mundane life indifferent to empires/politics: rain, debts, aching backs, daily tasks continue
- Mystery and obscurity: Boulatruelle's forest searching, officer rescue, wagon woman, identity/purpose concealed
- Hidden transgressions and buried truths: mill ledgers rewritten, letters burned, debts owed
- Civilian resistance masked by obedience: Bourbons misread soldier compliance as popular consent
- Human resilience through adaptation: ship metaphor for navigating multiple opposing forces
